passage: On the evening train out of Leipzig, Felix stared at the dark window and put a different question to himself. Not "which job is better?" but "which choice would I regret more in two years?" He pictured himself then, still in the tidy old role, doing the same reports, watching his friend Abebe's photos from the start-up's messy first office. That picture made his chest tighten. Then he pictured the start-up folding and himself job-hunting again. That one hurt too, but it felt like something he could recover from. He typed a note to Abebe: "Staying still is the bigger regret. I'm taking the risk." Abebe replied in seconds with a thumbs-up and "Bring snacks to the office."

qa.q: Which question did Felix ask himself on the train?
qa.a: He asked which choice he would regret more in two years.

qa.q: What is Felix feeling when he pictures staying in the old role?
qa.a: Felix feels a tightening dread, since the picture of the same reports two years on makes his chest tighten.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Felix add before accepting, and why?
qa.a: He could imagine the start-up closing and check what he could do next, because that shows whether the risk is survivable.

qa.q: How might Abebe see Felix's decision?
qa.a: Abebe, whose photos show the start-up's messy first office, replies in seconds with a thumbs-up, so Abebe seems glad to see Felix join.

grounding: Shows inversion: asking which decision would feel worse in two years and seeing that staying stagnant would be the bigger regret.

passage: In the office pantry during her last week as an intern, Damini stirred her tea and explained her dilemma to Usha, the senior analyst who had mentored her. "This company has offered me a permanent role. Stable, decent pay, the same reports I've done all summer. The start-up has offered me a product role. Exciting, but they might not exist in two years." Usha said, "Flip it. Imagine two years from now. Which choice would you regret more?" Damini closed her eyes. She pictured herself here, still making the same weekly report, only a little faster. Then she pictured the start-up folding, and herself job-hunting with two years of messy, real experience. "The first one," she said slowly. "Staying and not growing feels worse than trying and it falling apart." Usha smiled. "Then you have your answer. Talk it over at home too."

qa.q: What role did the start-up offer?
How did Damini feel picturing herself still making the same report?
qa.a: Damini felt a sinking sense of regret, seeing that staying and not growing would feel worse than a start-up failing.

qa.q: What else could Damini do before accepting the start-up?
qa.a: Damini could ask the start-up how long it expects to run and what happens if it closes, so the risk is clearer.
Usha doesn't choose for Damini but offers the regret question, which lets Damini find her own answer.

grounding: Shows a graduate asking which choice would feel worse in two years and seeing that a stagnant role would be a bigger regret than a shaky start-up.

passage:
Subject: my decision (and how I got there)
Parveen Didi,
You told me to stop making lists and ask one question: which choice would I regret more in two years? I tried it last night, and it worked.
Option 1: stay at the bank's back office, where I interned. Stable, secure, the same reconciliation work every day. Option 2: join the ed-tech start-up as their fourth engineer. It could shut down.
I pictured two years ahead. In the first picture, I'm still at the same desk, faster at the same task, telling myself "next year I'll switch." In the second, the start-up has folded, and I'm job-hunting with two years of building real features.
The first picture felt worse. Much worse. A shaky start-up that fails still leaves me with skills; a stagnant job just leaves me older.
I'm accepting the start-up tomorrow. Please help me explain it to Papa.
Anand

qa.q: What would Anand be at the start-up?
How did Anand feel about the first picture?
qa.a: Anand felt it was much worse, a heavy regret at staying stuck at the same desk.

qa.q: What else could Anand do before accepting?
qa.a: Anand could ask the start-up about its plans for the coming year and talk it through with Papa alongside Parveen Didi, so the family understands the risk.

qa.q: How might Parveen Didi see the email?
qa.a: She would likely be pleased that her one-question advice helped, and ready to support Anand when talking to Papa.

grounding: Illustrates a graduate imagining two years ahead and deciding that a stagnant role would be a bigger regret than a start-up that might fail.
